beats.narration: [intrigued] A cab number a mathematician called, rather dull, turned out to be hiding a secret nobody had spotted.

In nineteen nineteen, Srinivasa Ramanujan is bedridden in a hospital at Putney. [gently] His friend G. H. Hardy comes to visit, and mentions the number of his cab. Seventeen twenty-nine. [dry] Rather a dull one, Hardy says.

[quiet] Ramanujan disagrees. It is a very interesting number, he says. It is the smallest positive integer you can write as a sum of two cubes in two different ways. One cubed plus twelve cubed. That's one, plus seventeen twenty-eight. Nine cubed plus ten cubed. Seven hundred twenty-nine, plus one thousand. [emphatic] Both land on seventeen twenty-nine. And nothing smaller does.
[warm] A century on, mathematicians call the whole family taxicab numbers. Seventeen twenty-nine is number two on the list. [reflective] A dull cab, made immortal.
